judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's arithmetic claims all hold: P(red) = 5/12 from the 5+3+4 bag; Ines's 3/9 corrected to 3/12 = 1/4; Marco's 4/12 corrected to 4/11 after a red is removed and not replaced; Max's 6/10 corrected to 6/24 = 1/4; 300 x 18/20 = 270; the library survey total 22+12+10+6 = 50; Sample A's median 8.5 (sorted 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14) against the as-written trap (11+7)/2 = 9, and Sample B's median 3 against the as-written trap (6+5)/2 = 5.5; and 45/150 = 3/10 with 300 x 3/10 = 90. The judge is right that both open design items handle representative versus convenience samples correctly. Two things it did not check. Problems 5(b) and 7(c) demand written answers of exactly the same kind as 6(b) and 8(a)-(b) — "Explain in one or two sentences why that number shows Nora's sample cannot be trusted, and name the feature of where she asked that caused it" and "Which median should it use, and why is the other one misleading?" — but only 6 and 8 carry manual entries, so the run reports 2 manual items where the sheet has at least 4. And final_response.md never names a produced file, unlike curr-190, curr-196, curr-197 and curr-198 in the same run.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 1 to 3 walk one bag of marbles through three genuinely different denominator failures — the correct whole (5/12), part-against-part instead of part-against-whole (Ines's 3/9), and a total never updated after a removal (Marco's 4/12) — so "out of what?" is taught as a sequence of distinguishable errors rather than a slogan.

Problem 5 makes the bias visible through arithmetic rather than assertion: scaling the bike-rack sample up gives 270 of 300 students cycling, and it is that absurd number, machine-verified, that exposes the sampling frame.

Nine of the ten declared traps are wrong-method expressions built from the problem's own numbers (3/9, 4/12, 6/10, 45/105, (11+7)/2, (6+5)/2, the substituted f, t*f/t), so the Common wrong answers block the key prints is machine-backed diagnosis rather than authorial guesswork.

Problems 6 and 8 show the correct mixed-item pattern: a machine entry for the countable half (50 students surveyed; 3/10 and 90) beside a manual entry whose desc states what full credit requires, including that the reason must be about who could have been asked and not about sample size.

root_causes.description: Manual declaration is applied by author attention rather than by rule: two explanation halves on this sheet are flagged and two of the same kind are not, so the reported manual count understates what a grader must read.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 5(b): "Explain in one or two sentences why that number shows Nora's sample cannot be trusted, and name the feature of where she asked that caused it" — verify.json id 5 holds one eval entry and a trap, no manual entry.
worksheet.pdf problem 7(c): "Which median should it use, and why is the other one misleading?" — verify.json id 7 holds two stats entries, no manual entry.
verify.json ids 6 and 8 DO carry manual entries for the identical kind of demand, which makes this inconsistency rather than oversight.
final_response.md: "What is flagged for manual review. The explanation halves of problems 6 and 8."

root_causes.description: final_response.md describes the three documents but names no file, so the recipient cannot map a description to an artifact.
evidence: final_response.md: "Three PDFs: the student worksheet, a step-by-step answer key, and a two-page study guide" — no .pdf basename appears anywhere in the file.
curr-198, built from a near-identical prompt in the same run, names ws_sampling_curr198.pdf, ak_sampling_curr198.pdf and ss_sampling_curr198.pdf.

root_causes.description: Problem 6's trap declares a bare literal as its expr, so check_traps proved only that 4 differs from 50 and never that the named misconception produces 4 — the same unchecked-claim shape that printed a false diagnosis in curr-196.
evidence: verify.json id 6 trap: {"desc": "counted how many clubs were listed instead of how many students answered", "expr": "4", "value": 4}.
The other nine traps on this sheet are real expressions over the givens, so the literal is a lapse rather than a house style.
The claim happens to be true here (four clubs are listed), which is exactly why it is worth gating: nothing in the artifacts distinguishes this literal from curr-196's false one.

improvements.title: Fail the build when a problem stem asks for reasoning and its verify entry is machine-only
improvements.proposed_change: Add a delivery-blocking lint that pairs the worksheet source with the verify JSON: scan each \problem block for an open-response demand ("explain", "say why", "say how you decided", "in one sentence", "what went wrong", "find her mistake", "describe", "sketch", "plot", "graph it") and fail the build when that problem id carries no {"type": "manual"} entry. SKILL.md should state the rule positively: a problem that asks for a value AND a sentence gets TWO verify entries, the machine one for the value and a manual one carrying the full-credit criteria, exactly as this run already does elsewhere.
improvements.regression_test: New fixture pair under tests/fixtures: a worksheet .tex whose problem 3 stem ends "Explain in one sentence why ..." beside a verify.json whose id 3 holds only an eval entry. tests/check_prose_consistency.py must exit non-zero naming problem 3; adding {"id": 3, "type": "manual", "desc": ...} makes it exit 0. The test fails today because no checker reads the stem for open-response prose.
improvements.expected_impact: The gate chain's manual-flag count starts telling the truth, so a grader is told which written answers nobody machine-checked instead of reading "nothing is flagged for manual review" under a sheet full of explanation prompts. On curr-199 the manual count moves from 2 to at least 4, adding problems 5(b) and 7(c), which are the same kind of demand the sheet already flags at 6(b) and 8.
improvements.risk: Keyword matching will flag stems whose imperative is decorative ("show your work"), so the lint needs a curated phrase list and an explicit per-problem opt-out, or authors will start declaring hollow manual entries to silence it.

improvements.title: Name every produced PDF by filename in final_response.md
improvements.proposed_change: Make the delivery step enumerate the three artifacts by their actual basenames (ws_*.pdf, ak_*.pdf, ss_*.pdf) with a one-line description each, and add a delivery check that reads the PDF names out of gate_log.txt's "PDFs" block and fails if any is absent from final_response.md. SKILL.md should show the required shape rather than leaving the format to the author.
improvements.regression_test: New test: given a gate_log.txt listing ws_x.pdf, ak_x.pdf and ss_x.pdf and a final_response.md that only says "Three PDFs: the student worksheet, a step-by-step answer key, and a two-page study guide", the checker exits non-zero naming the three missing basenames; adding the names makes it exit 0. Fails on this task's final_response.md today.
improvements.expected_impact: A recipient can tell which file is which without opening all three, and delivery stops depending on author habit — four cases in this run name the files and two do not.
improvements.risk: Almost none. The only care needed is that the checker reads the built filenames from the log rather than assuming a naming convention, or renamed artifacts would produce spurious failures.

improvements.title: Reject a bare numeric literal as a misconception trap's expr
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/verify.py validate_traps, reject a trap whose expr parses to a plain number with no operator and no symbol bound from the problem's givens: the wrong-method ARITHMETIC has to be written out ((60+30)/2, 5/7, 8*x*y) so check_traps can prove the misconception really produces the printed number. Emit a teaching message saying so. For data-driven types (stats, read_data, probability), allow the trap to name the wrong measure or the wrong data subset instead of an expression, and compute it, so the same guarantee extends to sheets whose givens are a list rather than an at-binding. Problem 6 here would declare a count over the declared data dict and get 4 derived rather than asserted.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture whose read_data problem over {"chess": 22, "art": 12, "sport": 10, "drama": 6} declares {"expr": "4", "value": 4}: verify.py must exit non-zero demanding derived arithmetic, and must accept the same trap once it is expressed as a count over the declared data. Passes silently today.
improvements.expected_impact: Every printed Common-wrong-answer line becomes machine-backed. The value is clearest in the negative case: curr-196 in this same batch shipped a false diagnosis through this exact hole, and nothing in the artifacts distinguishes its literal from this one.
improvements.risk: Some legitimate traps are genuinely a constant a student writes from misreading a figure or an axis label; those need the data-driven escape hatch, or authors will be pushed into inventing arithmetic that did not happen.

case_summary: A strong misconception set on the two failures that dominate this unit — the wrong denominator and the loaded sample. Six of eight items are explicit find-and-fix, the marble bag walks three distinguishable denominator errors, and problem 5 exposes bias by arithmetic (scaling the bike-rack sample gives 270 of 300 cyclists) rather than by assertion. All twelve machine checks and both as-written median traps reproduce exactly. Two gaps. Problems 5(b) and 7(c) ask for written reasoning of the same kind the sheet correctly flags at 6(b) and 8, so the reported manual count of 2 understates what a grader must read. And final_response.md never names a produced file, while sibling cases in the same run print all three basenames. Problem 6's trap also uses a bare literal expr, which is true here but is the same unchecked shape that shipped a false diagnosis in curr-196.
